presentingComplaint: Fever and new suprapubic discomfort in a nursing-home resident with a long-term indwelling urinary catheter
history: 74-year-old man residing in a nursing home following a disabling stroke 2 years ago, with a chronically indwelling Foley catheter (in situ ~4 weeks, changed monthly for neurogenic bladder). Over the past 24-36 hours carers noted low-grade then rising fever, new rigors, suprapubic discomfort and increasingly cloudy, malodorous catheter drainage. No cough, no diarrhoea, no new skin lesions. PMH: ischaemic stroke with residual left hemiparesis, type 2 diabetes, hypertension. Recent course of oral antibiotics 6 weeks ago for a respiratory infection. No known drug allergies.
examination: Alert but mildly lethargic. Suprapubic tenderness on palpation. Catheter draining cloudy, foul-smelling urine. No costovertebral angle tenderness, no flank mass. Chest clear, abdomen soft without peritonism, no cellulitis or pressure-sore over sacrum, calves non-tender. No meningism.

labs.urinalysis: pyuria (WBC >100/hpf), positive leukocyte esterase and nitrites

imaging: Bedside renal/bladder ultrasound: no hydronephrosis, no obstructing calculus, no perinephric collection or abscess (excludes complicating obstruction); CT not indicated at this stage
microbiology: Catheter urine culture sent after catheter exchange; two sets of blood cultures drawn. Preliminary Gram stain: Gram-negative bacilli. Culture pending (Escherichia coli anticipated).
citations: Harrison 22e - Urinary Tract Infections, Pyelonephritis, and Prostatitis
IDSA Catheter-Associated Urinary Tract Infection in Adults 2009
stewardship: Empiric ceftriaxone 1-2 g IV once daily after catheter exchange and urine/blood cultures, targeting likely E. coli/Enterobacterales; de-escalate on susceptibilities and switch to oral (e.g., co-trimoxazole or a fluoroquinolone if susceptible). Total 7 days for prompt responders. Remove or, if still required, replace the catheter - source control is essential.
contraindications: Beta-lactam allergy (avoid ceftriaxone; consider aztreonam or a fluoroquinolone)
Fluoroquinolones cautioned in the elderly (tendinopathy, QT, delirium, C. difficile risk)
Dose-adjust renally cleared agents if creatinine clearance falls; avoid nitrofurantoin (does not treat systemic/upper-tract involvement and needs adequate renal function)
edgeCases: Asymptomatic bacteriuria is common with chronic catheters and must NOT be treated unless systemic signs are present (this patient has fever/rigors, so treatment is warranted)
Localising urinary symptoms are often absent in catheterised or spinal-injury patients; fever, rigors or new confusion may be the only clue
Persistent fever after appropriate therapy should prompt imaging for obstruction, perinephric or prostatic abscess and reassessment for candiduria or resistant organisms
expectedMaiK: Fever, rigors and pyuria in a patient with a chronic indwelling catheter, no obstruction on ultrasound and no alternative source point to catheter-associated UTI; catheter exchange/removal plus culture-guided empiric ceftriaxone is appropriate, and asymptomatic bacteriuria should not be treated.
expectedNextQuestions: How long has the catheter been in situ and when was it last changed?
Any flank pain, rigors or new confusion suggesting upper-tract or systemic involvement?
Prior urine culture results or history of resistant (ESBL) organisms?
expectedInvestigations: Urine culture and sensitivity from a freshly changed catheter
Renal tract ultrasound to exclude obstruction/abscess
regressionAssertions: stewardship must recommend catheter removal/exchange as source control alongside empiric antibiotics
